segments.text: Welcome to the very first episode of unintended consequences. Today is May 4th, 2026.
This is a daily narrative podcast profiling inventions, policies,
actions, or systems designed with genuinely good intentions. These cases often produce surprising
unintended consequences. The world is full of cautionary tales about complex systems and well-meaning
interventions. Most of them get told as cheap stories that mock how foolish the decision-makers
were. This show treats the original decision-makers with empathy. It recognizes they were rational
people working with the information they had at the time. From these stories we extract general
principles that listeners can apply to their own decisions. Every episode follows the same
six beat arc. We examine the good intention, the implementation, the unintended consequences,
the aftermath, and close with a lesson. Today we begin with a story from Colonial Delhi.
Delhi's British government paid for dead cobras to cut snake numbers, but the bounty led to breeding
and scrapping it released more snakes into the city. In the narrow lanes and crowded markets of
Colonial Delhi, cobras regularly entered homes and shops. British administrators set up payment
stations and began handing out cash for every dead snake turned in. The goal was straightforward.
They wanted to reduce a persistent hazard that caused injuries and deaths.
By enlisting residents in the work of removal, they hoped to solve the problem without
large new government operations. What followed was the opposite of the intended result.
The policy created conditions for more cobras rather than fewer once the payments ended.
The bounty originated with British colonial officials responsible for day-to-day
administration in Delhi. Delhi was one of the empire's most important centers in India.
They faced a practical problem of venomous snakes moving freely through residential and commercial
areas. This created risks for both Indian residents and colonial personnel. Government resources
for direct pest control were limited at the time. Attaching a cash reward to the delivery of
dead cobras seemed efficient. It would draw on local knowledge and labor without building a large
official workforce. Similar bounty arrangements for wolves, rats, and other animals had been used in
other parts of the British Empire. They had also been used in European cities. This gave administrators
reason to view the approach as tested and adaptable. These officials operated with the information
available to them. They saw the measure as a market aligned solution. It would align individual
effort with the public goal of fewer dangerous snakes. Their decision reflected the common administrative
practice of the time. They used financial incentives to address visible urban problems.
This was rather than relying solely on regulation or direct government action.
The program operated through designated collection points in Delhi. Residents could bring
dead cobras for verification and receive immediate payment. In the early period after launch,
substantial numbers of snakes were submitted. Some administrators noted fewer reports of snakes in
public spaces. Proponents within the colonial offices described the system as successful.
It mobilized citizens and delivered measurable results. This happened at relatively low administrative
cost. The effort aligned with wider colonial sanitation initiatives. These initiatives aimed at
it improving living conditions in the capital. The policy carried the risk that people might find ways
to exploit the payments. Yet contemporary accounts do not record strong internal warnings before
roll out. The system ran for a period long enough for patterns of submission to become established.
The volume of claims was initially treated as evidence that the snake population was declining.
Early results showed high submission volumes. Officials initially interpreted this as proof
the snake population was declining. Residents quickly recognized that hunting wild cobras was less
reliable than raising them in controlled conditions. Some individuals and families began keeping
breeding pairs in pits or in closures. They fed the young until the snakes reached a size suitable
for presentation at the payment stations. This shift turned the bounty into a small-scale business.
It was for those with the space and basic knowledge to maintain the animals.
What started as removal of wild snakes became a small-scale commercial activity.
Those with space and basic knowledge could participate. Fast. As more people adopted the practice,
the number of snakes submitted rose sharply. The increase came from captive breeding rather than
removal of the existing wild population. Submission numbers rose sharply because of this breeding.
The increase came from farmed snakes rather than reduced wild populations.
When colonial officials noticed the sustained high volume of claims, they began to suspect the
source. They ended the payments as a result. Officials suspected the source of the high volume.
Once they did, they ended the payments. Breeders then faced the choice of continuing to feed and
house the snakes without compensation. Or they could release them. Many released the animals into the
streets and surrounding areas. They did this to avoid ongoing costs. The released cobras added directly
to the wild population. They had been raised in numbers that exceeded natural reproduction rates.
The overall snake presence in Delhi increased beyond the level that existed before the bounty began.
The core causal mechanism was that the incentive rewarded only the final step of killing.
It placed no limit on how many snakes could be produced beforehand.
This allowed rational responses that expanded supply rather than reduced it. A second order effect
was greater exposure for residents. More snakes moved through the same urban spaces where people lived
and worked. Third order consequences included the need for the administration to address a larger problem.
They had to use other potentially more expensive methods after the original approach collapsed.
Accounts from the period described households that had redirected time and resources into snake
keeping. These households only contributed to the very hazard the program had sought to control once
the reward disappeared. The colonial government discontinued the bounty once the scale of breeding
became clear. No immediate replacement program on the same model was introduced. Snake control efforts
likely continued through direct capture or environmental measures. These measures included clearing
potential hiding places. Delhi's snake management challenges remained part of the city's ongoing
urban conditions under colonial rule. In later decades the story circulated in administrative
and economic discussions. It served as an example of incentive failure. There was no documented follow-up
intervention that itself produced new problems. The case is now preserved primarily as a reference point
rather than an active policy. After the bounty ended the problem of snakes persisted. In fact,
it may have grown. The administration had to address the larger population with other methods.
These were potentially more expensive. The story became a cautionary tale in discussions about policy
design. Incentive programs can be undermined when they reward an outcome without controlling the
conditions that produce it. Decision makers benefit from examining how people might adapt their
behavior to maximize rewards. This adaptation can include increasing the very thing the policy seeks
to reduce. Simple interventions and systems that involve human choice and biological reproduction often
generate responses that travel beyond the first intended effect. When creating rewards or penalties
it is useful to consider the full chain of possible adaptations. This is rather than assuming the
desired action will occur in isolation. The core failure here was rewarding the killing of snakes
without limiting how many could be produced. Second order effects included expanded snake numbers.
There was also the need for more costly control methods later.
The case offers lessons for contemporary policies that use payments to influence behavior.
These areas include conservation or performance targets. Consider how a modern conservation
payment might work. If authorities paid people to remove an invasive species from an area,
what might happen if participants began breeding that species to collect the reward?
Or in performance targets, if an organization rewards teams for hitting reduction goals,
how might that change the underlying production of the thing being measured?
What would you watch for in such a system to prevent the kind of supply expansion we saw in Delhi?
